title: Japan and NASA's MMX Spacecraft Is Headed to Phobos to Bring Back the First Samples From Another Planet's Moon
excerpt: JAXA's MMX spacecraft launched Oct. 19 toward Mars's moons. It will land on Phobos, collect at least 10 grams of material, and return the first samples from a moon of another planet in 2031.
content:
A Japanese spacecraft carrying NASA instruments is on its way to the moons of Mars, on a mission to do something no space agency has ever done: land on the moon of another planet, collect its soil, and bring samples back to Earth.

The Martian Moons eXploration mission — MMX — lifted off on October 19, 2026, aboard an H3 rocket from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan. About 71 minutes after liftoff, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) confirmed the spacecraft had separated from the rocket and was on its planned trajectory, according to Astronomy Magazine.

A long stay at Mars

MMX is due to arrive at Mars in August 2027. It will study both of the planet's moons — Phobos and Deimos — deploy the Franco-German IDEFIX rover onto Phobos, and touch down on Phobos itself as many as two times to collect at least 10 grams of surface material.

Settling a long-running question

Scientists still do not know where Mars's moons came from. They may be asteroids captured by the planet's gravity, or debris blasted into orbit by an ancient giant impact. Analyzing real Phobos material in laboratories on Earth could settle the question. If the mission succeeds, the samples will be the first ever returned from a moon of another planet; they are due back on Earth in 2031.

NASA's role

NASA is a partner in the mission, contributing the MEGANE gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer — developed by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory — along with a pneumatic sampling device, communications support, and participating scientists, according to NASA and Scientific American.
